headline: Somatropin
punch: Why the high arm was the right arm.

headline: The two doses tested
body: Mauras randomised GH-deficient adolescents to **0.3 or 0.7 mg/kg per week**, given as daily subcutaneous injections, and followed them to near-adult height. | Note what 0.7 per week actually is when you divide it by seven: **0.1 mg/kg per day**. The dose people argue about is not an extrapolation. It is a trial arm with a published adult-height result.
punch: 0.7 per week is 0.1 per day. It was tested.

headline: 4.6 centimetres
body: The high dose group were significantly taller at near-adult height by **4.6 cm**, P < 0.001, n = 75, 95% CI 2.6 to 6.5. | In those treated at least four years the gap was **5.7 cm**. First-year growth rate was **9.8 cm/yr** against 8.2 on standard dose, P = 0.001. The longer it ran, the wider it got.
punch: _The gap grew with time on the dose._

headline: Bone age did not move
body: The main argument against pushing the dose is that you spend your plates faster. Both studies that measured it say otherwise. | Mauras: bone ages advanced **approximately 1 year per chronological year in both groups**, and high dose **did not increase the rate of skeletal maturation**. Nwosu followed 71 children up to 14 years: BA minus CA was -1.05 at start and -0.69 at end, **P = 0.09**.
punch: ==The cost everyone fears was measured, twice, and was not there.==

headline: Higher still
body: Lundberg randomised children to 33 or **67 µg/kg/day** and found pubertal height gain and adult height SDS **greater on the high dose**. High GH dose was one of the variables explaining 63% of adult height variance. | Then their own conclusion: the high dose was set at 67 **even though the present results suggest that nearly 50% of the children could have benefitted from an even higher dose**.
punch: Their own read: half of them needed more than the high arm.

headline: Why that is not reckless
body: Lundberg: **no dose-dependent adverse event involving carbohydrate metabolism was observed, which confirms previous studies with high GH doses**. | Mauras: high dose rhGH was **well tolerated, with a similar safety profile as standard dose** and no difference in HbA1c or glucose between groups. Two trials, both looking for a metabolic penalty at the high arm, neither finding an adverse event.
punch: Markers moved. Adverse events did not.

headline: The markers that did move
body: Being straight about it: Mauras found a greater increase in **fasting insulin, P = 0.011**, and **C-peptide, P = 0.019**, on the high dose. And **28%** of the high dose group had IGF-1 above the normal range at any time, against 9% on standard. | So the high arm is not free. It costs you insulin sensitivity drift and IGF-1 overshoot, both of which are measurable and both of which are manageable.
punch: Two things to monitor, not two reasons to stop.

headline: Thyroid is not optional
body: GH upregulates type 2 deiodinase, pulling T4 across into T3. **Free T4 declines significantly**, by about 1.09 pmol/L, because the conversion consumes it. | And GH blunts TSH pulsatility and TRH sensitivity, so the number you would screen with is pushed down by the drug causing the problem. In hypopituitary adults this unmasked central hypothyroidism in **36 to 47%** who looked euthyroid beforehand.
punch: ==Up to half developed it. A normal TSH will not catch it.==

headline: Replace the T4
body: If the mechanism is T4 being consumed faster than it is replaced, the intervention follows directly from the mechanism. Monitor **free T4 and free T3**, not TSH, because TSH is the parameter this drug suppresses. | This is the single most predictable requirement on high-dose GH, and it has an unambiguous mechanism behind it rather than an inferred one.
punch: Screen free T4. Replace what the conversion drains.

headline: Protect insulin sensitivity
body: The documented metabolic cost is reduced insulin sensitivity, so the countermeasure is agents that improve it. **Empagliflozin**, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and **imeglimin**, which works on mitochondrial function in the beta cell and on peripheral sensitivity, both act on that axis. | Be clear on the evidence grade: these are established insulin-sensitivity agents, and no trial has tested either alongside GH for this purpose. Mechanism sound, combination untested.

headline: Time it to the window
body: Subcutaneous, at bedtime, is the administration used across these trials. It puts the dose into the window when somatostatin has naturally withdrawn and your own largest pulse occurs. | And keep carbohydrate away from it: a pre-bed carbohydrate load flattens the nocturnal slow-wave-sleep GH surge, which is the largest physiological pulse you have.
punch: Bedtime, subcutaneous, and not on top of carbs.

headline: Where the data stops
body: No trial here tested above **0.7 mg/kg/week** to an adult-height endpoint. Lundberg's statement supports going above 67 µg/kg/day; it does not identify an optimum, and nobody has found the top of the curve. | And every number in this monograph is from children with a diagnosed growth disorder and open plates. None of it describes an adult with an intact axis.
punch: Supported up to the high arm. Above it is inference.

headline: Verdict
body: The high arm won on adult height by 4.6 cm, won by more the longer it ran, did not advance bone age in either study that checked, and produced no carbohydrate adverse event in either trial. The trialists themselves said half their patients needed more. | It is not free: insulin markers drift and IGF-1 overshoots in about a quarter of people. Both are monitorable. Thyroid is the one that hides, and free T4 is the number that finds it.
punch: ==High dose, bedtime, subcutaneous. Watch free T4 and insulin.==
